extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners (caricature artists, historians, designers) seeking an overview of caricature
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic overview of caricature as an art form: its definition, history, purposes, artistic elements, computational approaches, and recognition properties. Useful for someone learning how caricatures are made, why they work, and how they vary stylistically and technically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: exaggeration or simplification of features
rubrics_metrics.description: A caricature is a rendered image showing the features of its subject in a simplified or exaggerated way through sketching, pencil strokes, or other artistic drawings (compare to: cartoon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used both as portraits of recognizable individuals and as comic illustrations; can be insulting or complimentary and may serve political or entertainment purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose / intent (insulting, complimentary, political, entertainment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricatures can be either insulting or complimentary, and can serve a political purpose, be drawn solely for entertainment, or for a combination of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political cartoons commonly use caricatures of politicians; movie-star caricatures are often found in entertainment magazines. The intended purpose influences tone, subject selection, and distribution venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizability / portrait-of-a-person focus
rubrics_metrics.description: In modern usage, 'caricature' is used predominantly for a portrait of a recognizable individual (much as originally used to describe works of Pier Leone Ghezzi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful caricature typically preserves enough likeness to make the subject identifiable while exaggerating salient features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of features to exaggerate: natural, acquired, and vanities
rubrics_metrics.description: A caricaturist draws on (1) the natural characteristics of the subject (the big ears, long nose, etc.); (2) the acquired characteristics (stoop, scars, facial lines etc.); and (3) the vanities (choice of hair style, spectacles, clothes, expressions, and mannerisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining these categories helps determine which traits to emphasize; examples given include ears, nose, scars, hairstyles, spectacles and habitual expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone / ethical impact: mock versus wound
rubrics_metrics.description: The caricaturist can choose to either mock or wound the subject with an effective caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit artistic/ethical choice: caricature can be gentle mockery (entertainment) or biting satire intended to injure reputation or critique; choice affects stylistic aggressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brennan formalization: exaggeration relative to an average face (norm-based exaggeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature formalized as the process of exaggerating differences from an average face: subtract the corresponding point on the mean face, scale the difference by a factor larger than one, and add the scaled difference back onto the mean face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brennan's system required a frontal drawing with a standardized topology; it operationalizes exaggeration as scaling deviation from a norm. Applicable to algorithmic / partially automated caricature generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population-variance-aware exaggeration (Mo et al. refinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The population variance of each facial feature should be taken into account: features that vary little (e.g., inter-eye distance) should be exaggerated even for small deviations, whereas features with large variance (e.g., nose size) need larger deviations to warrant exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This refines norm-based methods by weighting exaggeration according to how diagnostic a feature is across the population; it guides which deviations are worth amplifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist-specific style and example-based mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature varies depending on the artist and cannot be captured in a single definition; systems can learn and mimic the style of a particular caricature artist given training pairs of photos and corresponding caricatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitates an individual artist's chosen distortions, line work, and stylistic conventions; implies that successful caricature may be judged by faithfulness to a stylistic tradition or the artist's recognizable signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pose and viewpoint considerations (frontal vs three-quarters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most computer systems are restricted to exactly frontal poses, whereas many manually produced caricatures choose an off-center 'three-quarters' view; Brennan's drawings were frontal-pose line drawings, while manual artists often use varied poses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of pose affects recognizability and expressive potential; three-quarters views are common in manual caricature and may better capture personality than strictly frontal automated approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/medium constraints (computer vs traditional methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer graphic systems require different skills and can produce finer coloring textures, but are not necessarily simpler; many systems have style and pose limitations compared to human artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated tools may limit pose, require standardized inputs, or fail to reach the expressive quality of human work; conversely, they can enable new styles (geometric distortions of photographs) and scalability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition effectiveness (recognition advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding: caricatures were recognised more accurately than the original images (demonstrated with line drawings and photographic-quality images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by norm-based and exemplar-based theories of face recognition; recognizability is an evaluative metric for caricature success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and context of production (street caricature / souvenir use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary caricatures are often used as gifts or souvenirs, drawn quickly for patrons at street fairs, carnivals, boardwalks and events for a small fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this context, time-efficiency and immediate entertainment value are key quality criteria; style may be simplified, and turnaround time (a few minutes) is an explicit constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as political communication and campaigning tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically and modernly, caricature has been a valuable tool for political campaigning and satire, used to attack or critique public figures and policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used politically, clarity of message, recognizability of target, and rhetorical exaggeration are importance criteria; historically influential works (e.g., Gillray) illustrate these functions.
